title: Chapter 108 – Missing Pages
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Ye]

Ye has spent forty years being underestimated, and she has come to regard it as the most useful instrument she owns.

She climbs the ridge road at the third bell of the afternoon, three days after the sky opened, in a plain gray robe with her braid pinned flat and her scroll case under her arm, and no one looks at her twice. An old woman. A scholar. A keeper of dusty rooms. The porters on the stair step aside without raising their eyes. The gate-wardens of the ridge-houses bow to her out of a habit older than their service, and turn at once to the young man at her side.

Lin Jian walks half a pace behind her, in the Silver Leaf's gray, with the white jade tag at his throat.

He has grown into the tag. That is what she thinks, glancing at him sidelong as they pass under the first arch. Four years ago he was a thin dark boy with the stoop of a clerk. Now he walks like a man who has been struck many times and does not mean to be struck again. He carries himself lightly. His eyes go everywhere. And every so often, when he thinks she is not looking, his gaze blurs for a breath, and she knows he is looking at something that is not there.

The Door in Autumn, she thinks. Two points of energy, and a strain on the Seal. He is reading the road.

She has not told him to stop. She has told him to be careful.

"The Cloud Peak Hall," she says aloud, as they come out onto the ridge, "was founded by the third Elder of the Azure Cloud Sect, a man of the Shen line, two hundred and eleven years after the Founders departed. It has produced six Core disciples, four Elders, and a Sect Head. It has never lost a seat on the floor." She does not slow. "It is very proud of its manners."

"I have noticed."

"Do not underestimate them for that. A family that never raises its voice has never needed to."

"I will remember."

"You will also remember to drink the tea," she says dryly. "Whatever it is. A refusal is a statement."

"I was not planning to refuse."

"Good." The corner of her mouth moves. "You are learning."

* * *

The ridge-house gate is guarded by a man she knows, and does not like.

Shen Yuhang stands at the foot of the white steps in his silver-edged gray, with his sword at his hip and his hands behind his back. He has not changed in three years. Thirty now, or near it, pale and carved and impeccably dressed, with the jade pin in his hair and the same pale eyes. He greets her with a bow of perfect depth. He greets the Gate Bearer with a bow that is exactly one finger shallower.

"Elder Ye," he says. "Silver Leaf Lin. My brother awaits you."

"Silver Leaf Shen," says Jian.

"Foundation Middle, I hear. My congratulations." He says it as a man says a word in a language he is learning. "I am told the sky was remarkable. I was in the training yard. I dropped my sword."

"I am sorry to have startled you."

"Not at all. It was educational." A pause. "I trust you will give my brother a fair hearing. He is, I think, a more patient man than I."

"I am sure he is."

They look at one another. It is the look of two men who have been counting each other's steps for three years, and Ye, standing between them with her scroll case in the crook of her arm, feels the old dry sensation of a war that nobody has declared. She taps her stick on the step.

"The tea," she says, "is getting cold."

Shen Yuhang's eyes flick to her. Something moves in them, very quick, and is gone. He bows again, shallower than before.

"By all means, Elder. Please."

He steps aside. As she passes, she catches, for the barest instant, a smell on his robe that she has smelled before. A faint, dry, sweetish smell, like plum bark. It is gone in a breath.

So he too, she thinks. Everyone in this house.

* * *

The ridge-house is built of white stone, and it is the quietest building she has ever entered.

It stands at the end of a long avenue of cypress, in a bowl of the hills where the wind does not reach, and its roofs are tiled in a dull silver that gives back no light. There are no banners. There is no sound. The courtyard they cross is paved in smooth stone, raked into patterns that nobody has walked on. Servants in white move along the colonnades on soft shoes, and every one of them keeps their eyes lowered.

Ye notes it all. She notes the absence of birds. She notes that the cypresses have been trimmed so evenly that they look like the teeth of a comb. She notes that the stone of the hall, on closer view, is not white at all, but a pale cold gray, the color of old bone, and that where the sun strikes it, it seems to drink the light.

Quiet, she thinks. Too quiet.

They are shown into a tea room on the east side.

It is a plain, elegant space, with a floor of pale wood and a low table and three cushions, and a window onto a garden of raked gravel and a single stone. A man sits on the far cushion, kneeling, with his hands in his lap. He rises as they enter.

He is tall, and thin, and somewhere past thirty-five. The same pale eyes as his brother. The same carved, quiet face. But where Shen Yuhang is a drawn blade, this man is a sheathed one. His robe is white, plain, with a narrow silver border. He wears no sword. He wears no ornament but a single ring of dark jade on his left hand. And when he smiles, it is so gentle, so entirely unforced, that for a breath Ye forgets what she knows.

"Elder Ye," says Shen Yuxian. "You honor the Hall. And the Gate Bearer." He bows. "I am glad you have come. Please. Sit."

* * *

The tea is the finest she has ever tasted.

She says so, with the brusque courtesy of a woman who has been served a great deal of tea in a great many halls, and Shen Yuxian inclines his head, and says that it is a leaf from the northern terraces, picked in the first week of the thaw, and that he will send a pound to the Sutra Hall. She does not thank him. She drinks.

For a quarter hour they talk of nothing.

He asks after the Sutra Hall's new roof. He asks after the school, and the herbal room, and a girl named Yue whom he has heard is gifted. He asks about the cold winter and the dry spring and the state of the northern roads. He does not mention the sky. He does not mention the Gate. He is a perfect host, courteous, attentive, a little shy, and Ye finds herself, against all her instincts, growing easy.

That is the technique, she thinks sharply. It is a very good one.

Across the table, Lin Jian sits with his cup in both hands and his eyes lowered. He has said perhaps twenty words. His face is blank and polite. But she sees his gaze lift, once, as Shen Yuxian turns to refill the pot, and rest for a long moment on the Core disciple's face. His pupils widen. Then it drops.

He has read him. She would stake her chair on it.

"I have been in seclusion for a long time," says Shen Yuxian, setting down the pot. "I find I have lost the knack of conversation. Forgive me if I am abrupt." He folds his hands. "The sky three days ago was remarkable. I saw it from the courtyard. I have not seen the like since my own breakthrough, and mine was smaller."

"It was a Foundation breakthrough," says Jian. "A middling one."

"With a violet-gold ray, over an alchemist's furnace? In the middle of winter?" The pale eyes are kind. "Gate Bearer, I think you do yourself a disservice. I think you drew the attention of the heavens."

"I think the heavens have better things to do."

"One would hope." A smile. "But I wonder if you know why."

"I do not."

"Nor do I." He opens his hands. "I only wanted to say that the Cloud Peak Hall has been, perhaps, a poor neighbor to you. My brother's challenge was unwise. I told him so. I have spent nine years learning the value of patience, and I should like to offer you a gift of it." He pauses. "The Hall will withdraw its objections to your standing. It will withdraw its pressure on the Tan family. It will withdraw, in short, from your road."

Ye sets down her cup.

"And in return?" she says.

"I beg your pardon?"

"A gift has a giver's price, Shen Yuxian. I am old, but I am not simple."

"Of course." He bows his head, and when he lifts it the smile has not changed, but there is something quieter beneath it. "In return, I should like a small thing. A pill. The recipe for what the Gate Bearer took. The Nine Turn. I understand it is Elder Bai's work." His eyes move to Jian. "The Hall has an elder who is dying. He has been dying for eleven years. I should like to help him."

* * *

It is, Ye thinks, almost too neat.

She watches Jian. He holds the cup. He does not drink. His face is as still as stone, and she is aware, in the way a woman is aware of a clock ticking in a silent house, of the thoughts passing behind it.

The pill is not Bai's alone. It is a Founders' recipe, from the vault. If he gives it, he gives the vault. If he refuses, he is an enemy.

"The Nine Turn is Elder Bai's," says Jian at last, quietly. "I cannot give what is not mine. But I will take the request to him."

"That is all I ask."

"And I will ask something in return."

Shen Yuxian's brows rise a hair.

"Your elder," says Jian. "The one who is dying. I should like to see him."

The silence in the tea room is complete.

Ye does not move. She does not breathe. She has not decided yet whether she is horrified or delighted. It is exactly the thing she would have asked, had she dared, and exactly the thing a careful man would not.

"Why?" says Shen Yuxian softly.

"Because a pill is a poor gift for a man I have not examined." Jian meets his eyes. "I am not a physician. But I have read many kinds of illness in the last few years, and I would like to know what you are asking me to cure."

A long moment. A bird that was not there before begins to sing in the garden, one note, then silence.

"I will consider it," says Shen Yuxian.

He pours again. The tea is steaming, jade green in the white cup. He does not look at Jian when he speaks, but at the garden beyond the window, the raked gravel and the single stone.

"The Elder you ask about is very old," he says. "He has not spoken in many years. He does not see visitors. It is not a matter of pride. It is a matter of the family's grief." A small pause. "I have sat at his side for eleven years, and it has taught me a certain humility about what can be mended."

"I understand."

"Do you?" The pale eyes come round. "You are young. You have the confidence of a man who has not yet lost much. I do not say it unkindly." He takes up his cup. "But I will tell you what I have learned. Some things are not hurt. They are kept. There is a difference, and it is worth knowing."

Jian says nothing. His face is quite still.

Ye watches the cup rise to the Core disciple's lips. She watches the throat move. She sees, as she has not seen before, the slight tension in the shoulder, the flicker at the corner of the eye. She thinks: he is afraid. Not of them. Of something behind them. Of someone in a far room who will be told, tonight, what was said.

So even the Cloud Peak Hall has a master.

He rises. "The tea has gone cold. Elder Ye, I would be honored if you would see our library while the Gate Bearer and I finish our business. It is considered the second finest in the Sect."

"I have heard so."

"I think you will find some items of interest." He smiles. "My servant will show you."

He means to separate them. She knows it. She knows that Jian knows it. Their eyes meet across the table, and she gives him the smallest nod. Go on.

She rises, and bows, and follows the servant into the cool white corridor.

* * *

The corridor is white, and cool, and very long.

The servant walks half a pace ahead on soft shoes, a slight young man with a shaven head and downcast eyes. Ye walks behind, leaning a little on her stick, though she needs it less than she lets people believe. She does not speak. She studies the walls. They are blank, without scroll or painting or lamp, and she notes that every twelve paces there is a small round recess in the stone, no larger than a coin, with a dull black disc set into it.

Sensors, she thinks. Or something worse.

"Forgive me," she says, as though to herself. "My eyes are not what they were. What are those?"

"Ornaments, Elder."

"Of what?"

"I could not say." The servant's voice is level and without color. "I was told only to keep the corridor clear."

"A fine old tradition." She taps her stick. "I once knew a clerk who kept corridors clear for forty years. He swore he never saw a thing."

The servant says nothing. But his step falters, a fraction, on the stone.

Clerk, she thinks. He knows the word.

She does not press. She files it, with the smell on Shen Yuhang's robe and the plum-bark paper and the scent of camphor. A scholar's mind is a long room of small cabinets, and she has spent forty years labeling them.

* * *

The library of the Cloud Peak Hall is a long room under a barrel vault, and for the first ten minutes she believes that she has misjudged them.

It is superb. Shelf upon shelf of black lacquer, ranks of gray silk-bound volumes, a hundred rolled maps in a rack, a reading table of polished wood. There is a section on the history of the Hall. There is a section on law. There is a case of manuscripts from the southern provinces that she has been trying to borrow for eleven years. She walks the room slowly, trailing her fingers along the spines, and her heart beats a little faster than is dignified.

The servant stands at the door and watches her with lowered eyes.

She pretends to browse. She pulls a volume at random, reads a line, replaces it. She works her way to the back, to the last alcove, where the lamplight does not reach, and there, on a low shelf behind a lacquer screen, she finds what she did not know she was looking for.

It is a row of narrow books, bound in gray, without titles. Plain boards. A cord of undyed hemp. Each volume is the size of a man's hand, and there are thirty of them, shelved in a line, and the spine of every one is stamped with the same device: a small black square with nothing in it.

Plum-bark, she thinks. The faint sweetish smell is unmistakable.

She takes down the first.

It is a ledger. The pages are ruled in red. The hand is small, exact, trained, with the loops of the d closed and the stroke lifting at the end of each word, and every line records a date, a number, and a sum. Year 487. Fourth month. Tan: 12 stones. Zhou: 40. She turns pages. Year 493. Fifth month. Mu: 6 stones. Gu: 3. Names, or fragments of names. Initial letters. A column of numbers that run on and on down the pages like a procession of ants.

A payroll, she thinks. Six hundred years of it.

She puts it back with a shaking hand and takes down the one at the end of the row.

* * *

The last book is thicker than the others, and newer. It has been recently handled. Its cover is warm.

She opens it standing in the dim alcove, and reads the first page, and feels her knees go weak.

The Roll of the Keepers.

It is not a ledger. It is a list. A short list, in a firm bold hand that is not the clerk's, written on heavy cream paper, under a header that she has seen only once before in her life, in a scratched line of old ink in a vault three flights beneath the Sutra Hall. A column of names. Each is struck through, save one. First: Wei Anzhi. Died year 7. Second: Su Linghua. Died year 61. On and on, names she has never read, spanning six hundred years. And at the bottom, in fresher ink, the last two entries.

Thirtieth: Gu Mingzhe. Died year 440.

Thirty-first: Sang Ruo. Taken. Year 441.

Her breath stops.

She stares at the name on the thirty-first line.

Sang Ruo.

The scholar. The finest mind of her generation, a Core disciple at twenty, who had walked into the Sutra Hall one morning forty years ago and picked up a brush and taught a stammering girl of twenty-eight how to read a ledger. Who had been warm, and dry, and merciless, and kind. Who had said, on the last night, in a voice Ye has heard in her sleep every night since:

Beware the ones who wear no names.

Taken. Year 441.

She does not know what the date means. But Sang Ruo disappeared in the year 441 of the Sect's calendar, forty years ago. Her name is on this list, thirty-first of the Keepers, under the word taken.

Not died, she thinks. Taken. She grips the book in both hands. They did not say she died. They said she was taken.

Taken from the Sect, or taken up? Seized, or chosen? The word will bear either meaning, and the hand that wrote it has left no sign. Her teacher's name is the last on a list of those who hold the House, and the line beneath it is blank.

My teacher was a Keeper of the House. She cannot breathe. And I do not know whether she is its prisoner or its master.

* * *

The page below holds a second thing, and it takes her a long moment to understand it.

It is a drawing. A floor plan, in thin black ink, of a building she knows: the Law Pavilion. The Council Floor, the round room, the pool, the seven cushions in a ring. Six of them are marked with a small neat character: Mu. Zhou. Ye. Bai. Shen Wuye. Qin Hao. And the seventh, the empty cushion, the seat of the Sect Head who has been in seclusion for eleven years, has a mark of its own.

It is a black square. Nothing in it.

And beside it, in a bold clear hand, a single line:

The Quiet Seat is held. Cast by proxy. Votes as the House directs.

Her mouth is dry.

Votes.

She remembers a hundred councils. She remembers Shen Wuye's voice reading the Sect Head's name aloud at the start of each, and the silence after, and the water in the pool never stirring. She remembers that the seventh stone has never been cast in a vote. The cushion is empty, they all say. The Head is in seclusion. It has been a fact of the Sect as solid as the mountain.

Votes as the House directs.

"Elder Ye," says the servant, from the end of the library, in a voice so soft that she barely hears it.

She closes the book. She slips it back on the shelf, between the others, in its place. She turns round with her hands folded in her sleeves and her face composed.

"The Core disciple has asked," says the servant, "if you would care to see the Quiet Hall."

* * *

It lies at the end of a corridor she did not know existed, behind a screen of white lacquer that slides aside with no sound.

A long cold room. A low ceiling. Rows of white lamps, burning with no flame. The air smells of camphor and ice and something else, something faintly sweet and faintly wrong. At the far end stands a bed.

It is not a bed. It is a slab of pale jade, the length of a man, set on a plinth, and the thing that lies on it is wrapped in white silk from throat to ankle. A pillow of folded linen under the head. A coverlet. Around the slab, at the four corners, stand four tall candles of white wax, and in the flame of each, if she looks closely, there is no heat.

Shen Yuxian stands at its side, with his hands folded.

"Our Head," he says gently. "He entered seclusion eleven years ago. In the great cold of that winter, it was thought wise to keep him warm. The Hall has tended him since." He bows toward the slab. "He is very old. He is very much loved."

She walks to the side of the jade.

The man on it is small, and withered, and impossibly aged. His head is shaved. His skin is the color of candle wax. His eyes are closed, and the lids are thin as paper, and she can see a faint blue pulse in the left temple, slow, slow, slow. A thread of black runs from the corner of his mouth, dried, and another along the line of the jaw. At the base of his skull, where the pillow lifts it, a small round knot of black cord is tied into the skin.

She knows what she is looking at. She has seen a thread-knot before, in a hall in Red Ridge, in a trial in the Law Pavilion, in a sheet of paper in Rong's hand.

It is a thread-knot. A very large one.

"He is not in seclusion," she says. Her voice is quite steady. She does not know where it comes from. "He is asleep."

"He is resting."

"He is held."

"Elder Ye." Shen Yuxian's smile is the gentlest thing she has ever seen. "I do not think you wish to say that in this room."

The white flames of the four candles do not flicker. Somewhere behind her, the lacquer screen slides closed, and she hears, in the silence, the soft precise click of a latch.

"I think," she says, "that I have a great deal of reading to do."

"Yes." He inclines his head. "I think you do."

She does not bow. She turns, instead, and looks once more at the withered face on the jade, the blue pulse in the temple, the black thread at the corner of the mouth. Eleven years. A Sect Head who has not been seen, not spoken, not voted, in all that time. And a cushion in a ring of seven, empty, with a stone cast in its name.

Votes as the House directs.

She lifts her chin, and walks out of the Quiet Hall on her own two feet, with her stick tapping softly on the pale floor, and does not look back until she is under the open sky.
